questions.prompt: Temperature and internal energy are…
questions.explanation: Temperature describes thermal state; internal energy includes microscopic kinetic and potential energy.

questions.prompt: Heat is energy transferred because of…
questions.explanation: Heating transfers energy from a hotter region to a cooler one.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of energy is the…
questions.explanation: Energy is in joules; watt is power, joules per second.

questions.prompt: A warm bath may have more internal energy than a hotter small cup because…
options: Higher temperature always means less internal energy
questions.explanation: Temperature alone does not determine total internal energy.

questions.prompt: During melting at fixed pressure, energy supplied can increase internal energy without increasing…
options: The potential part of internal energy
questions.explanation: Energy changes particle arrangement during the phase change.

questions.prompt: Using T/K = temperature/°C + 273, convert 0°C to kelvin. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: T = 0 + 273. This question uses the school approximation 273. Result: 273 K.

questions.prompt: Using T/K = temperature/°C + 273, convert 20°C to kelvin. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: T = 20 + 273. This question uses the school approximation 273. Result: 293 K.

questions.prompt: Using T/K = temperature/°C + 273, convert 37°C to kelvin. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: T = 37 + 273. This question uses the school approximation 273. Result: 310 K.

questions.prompt: Using T/K = temperature/°C + 273, convert 80°C to kelvin. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: T = 80 + 273. This question uses the school approximation 273. Result: 353 K.

questions.prompt: Using T/K = temperature/°C + 273, convert 100°C to kelvin. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: T = 100 + 273. This question uses the school approximation 273. Result: 373 K.

questions.prompt: Energy transfer through a stationary metal bar is mainly…
questions.explanation: Conduction involves microscopic interactions, including mobile electrons in metals.

questions.prompt: Warm water rising and cool water sinking is…
questions.explanation: Convection is energy transfer by bulk fluid motion.

questions.prompt: Which transfer mechanism needs no medium?
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation can cross a vacuum.

questions.prompt: Under the same radiation conditions, a matt black surface is generally a better absorber than…
options: A surface defined to be identical
questions.explanation: Surface properties affect absorption and emission; comparisons assume the same incident radiation.

questions.prompt: Why is convection not a heat-transfer mechanism within a solid block?
options: Its particles cannot undergo bulk fluid circulation
Gravity is always zero in solids
questions.explanation: Convection needs fluid movement; solids transfer through conduction and radiation at surfaces.

questions.prompt: A thermal radiation detector absorbs 600 J in 30 s. What is the average absorbed power? Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: Average power = energy/time = 600/30. Result: 20 W.

questions.prompt: A thermal radiation detector absorbs 1200 J in 60 s. What is the average absorbed power? Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: Average power = energy/time = 1200/60. Result: 20 W.

questions.prompt: A thermal radiation detector absorbs 900 J in 45 s. What is the average absorbed power? Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: Average power = energy/time = 900/45. Result: 20 W.

questions.prompt: A thermal radiation detector absorbs 2400 J in 80 s. What is the average absorbed power? Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: Average power = energy/time = 2400/80. Result: 30 W.

questions.prompt: A thermal radiation detector absorbs 500 J in 25 s. What is the average absorbed power? Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: Average power = energy/time = 500/25. Result: 20 W.

questions.prompt: Specific heat capacity describes energy needed to raise…
options: Any object by 100°C regardless of mass
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is energy per unit mass per temperature rise.

questions.prompt: The equation for warming without a phase change is…
questions.explanation: Use the temperature change, not the final temperature alone.

questions.prompt: Which unit can express specific heat capacity?
questions.explanation: J/(kg·K) is also valid because a temperature interval has the same numerical size.

questions.prompt: For equal mass and energy input, a larger c gives…
options: A necessarily higher final temperature in all cases
questions.explanation: ΔT = E/(mc).

questions.prompt: Ignoring heat losses when calculating c from supplied electrical energy usually…
options: Overestimates c if measured temperature rise is reduced by losses
questions.explanation: E_supplied exceeds energy gained by the sample; E_supplied/(mΔT) is too large if losses are ignored.

questions.prompt: Water has c = 4200 J/(kg·°C). Find the energy to warm 0.2 kg by 5°C, with no losses. Give the closest value.
Water has c = 4200 J/(kg·°C). Find the energy to warm 0.5 kg by 10°C, with no losses. Give the closest value.
Water has c = 4200 J/(kg·°C). Find the energy to warm 0.3 kg by 20°C, with no losses. Give the closest value.
Water has c = 4200 J/(kg·°C). Find the energy to warm 1 kg by 15°C, with no losses. Give the closest value.
Water has c = 4200 J/(kg·°C). Find the energy to warm 0.4 kg by 8°C, with no losses. Give the closest value.
Specific latent heat is energy per unit mass for…
options: A change of state at constant temperature under the stated conditions
questions.explanation: E = mL during a phase change.

questions.prompt: While pure ice melts at 0°C at atmospheric pressure, its temperature ideally…
options: Rises steadily through the entire phase change
Remains at 0°C until melting is complete
questions.explanation: Supplied latent energy changes the solid to liquid.

questions.prompt: To melt ice initially at −20°C, the total energy includes…
options: Warming the ice to 0°C, then melting it
No energy because ice is cold
questions.explanation: Add the sensible warming energy and latent melting energy.

questions.prompt: A temperature plateau on a heating curve can indicate…
options: Zero energy input in every case
questions.explanation: During a phase change, internal energy can rise while temperature stays fixed.

questions.prompt: Doubling the mass of ice already at 0°C doubles the ideal energy needed to melt it because…
options: Ice loses its mass as it melts
questions.explanation: Latent heat per unit mass remains fixed under the stated conditions.

questions.prompt: Ice is already at 0°C. With Lf = 334,000 J/kg, how much energy melts 0.1 kg completely? Give the closest value.
Ice is already at 0°C. With Lf = 334,000 J/kg, how much energy melts 0.2 kg completely? Give the closest value.
Ice is already at 0°C. With Lf = 334,000 J/kg, how much energy melts 0.3 kg completely? Give the closest value.
Ice is already at 0°C. With Lf = 334,000 J/kg, how much energy melts 0.4 kg completely? Give the closest value.
Ice is already at 0°C. With Lf = 334,000 J/kg, how much energy melts 0.5 kg completely? Give the closest value.
Two portions in thermal equilibrium have the same…
options: Total internal energy in every case
questions.explanation: Thermal equilibrium means no net thermal transfer between them.

questions.prompt: In an isolated mixing experiment, energy lost by the warm water equals…
options: Energy gained by the cool water
questions.explanation: Energy conservation relates the two changes, neglecting the container and losses.

questions.prompt: Equal masses of the same liquid at 80°C and 20°C mix without losses. The final temperature is…
questions.explanation: Equal heat capacities and masses give the arithmetic mean.

questions.prompt: If more cool water is used at the same initial temperatures, final temperature is generally…
options: Always closer to the hot starting temperature
Closer to the cool starting temperature
questions.explanation: The larger heat capacity weighs the final temperature towards its initial temperature.

questions.prompt: When may the simple weighted-temperature average fail?
options: When phase changes, heat loss or container heat capacity matter
Whenever the samples have equal c
questions.explanation: The simple formula assumes the same c, no phase change and an isolated system with negligible container capacity.

questions.prompt: Mix 0.2 kg of water at 80°C and 0.3 kg at 20°C. No losses, phase change or container heat capacity. Find Tf. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: For the same material, Tf = (m₁T₁ + m₂T₂)/(m₁ + m₂). Result: 44 °C.

questions.prompt: Mix 0.3 kg of water at 70°C and 0.2 kg at 20°C. No losses, phase change or container heat capacity. Find Tf. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: For the same material, Tf = (m₁T₁ + m₂T₂)/(m₁ + m₂). Result: 50 °C.

questions.prompt: Mix 0.1 kg of water at 90°C and 0.4 kg at 15°C. No losses, phase change or container heat capacity. Find Tf. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: For the same material, Tf = (m₁T₁ + m₂T₂)/(m₁ + m₂). Result: 30 °C.

questions.prompt: Mix 0.4 kg of water at 60°C and 0.1 kg at 10°C. No losses, phase change or container heat capacity. Find Tf. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: For the same material, Tf = (m₁T₁ + m₂T₂)/(m₁ + m₂). Result: 50 °C.

questions.prompt: Mix 0.2 kg of water at 75°C and 0.2 kg at 25°C. No losses, phase change or container heat capacity. Find Tf. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: For the same material, Tf = (m₁T₁ + m₂T₂)/(m₁ + m₂). Result: 50 °C.

questions.prompt: Power tells us the rate of…
questions.explanation: P = E/t; one watt is one joule per second.

questions.prompt: A 500 W heater operated for 20 s supplies…
If only 80% of heater energy enters the sample, useful sample energy is…
questions.explanation: Efficiency = useful output/input, so useful energy = efficiency × input.

questions.prompt: In E = mcΔT, a rise of 10°C is equivalent to a rise of…
questions.explanation: Intervals have equal numerical size on the Celsius and kelvin scales.

questions.prompt: To estimate the ideal heating time to warm and then melt a sample at fixed power, use…
options: Total required energy divided by power
questions.explanation: Add all required energy contributions, then use t = E/P.

questions.prompt: An ideal 200 W heater warms 0.1 kg of ice from −20°C to 0°C and then melts it. Use c_ice = 2100 J/(kg·°C) and Lf = 334000 J/kg. Find the time. Give the closest value.
questions.explanation: Total E = mc_ice × 20 + mLf, then t = E/P. No losses. Result: 188 s.

questions.explanation: Total E = mc_ice × 20 + mLf, then t = E/P. No losses. Result: 150 s.
